claims.text: Single-phase formation in noble-metal HEA nanoparticles is governed by kinetic limitation of atom or precursor mobility during phase formation.
Suppressing precursor mobility favors stochastic incorporation of multiple noble-metal species and formation of a random solid solution.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure or slow cooling creates excessive atomic mobility that permits elemental segregation and phase separation.
The proposed starting material contains more than five noble-metal single-source precursors.
A lower synthesis temperature can reduce the thermal budget and help inhibit precursor mobility.
A slower heating rate suppresses effective precursor mobility relative to rapid heating and cooling.
Minimizing dwell time at peak temperature limits atomic rearrangement.
Diffusion must be limited before the reducing agent completes the reaction to obtain the proposed kinetic trapping.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal systems containing more than five elements.
Restricted mobility kinetically freezes multiple elements into a crystal lattice before significant diffusion and phase separation occur.
Heating rate and dwell time control the activation energy available for atomic rearrangements.
Reducing the effective thermal budget through slower heating and minimal peak dwell will increase the fraction of uniform, single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
Reducing the effective thermal budget will provide control over the selected crystal structure.
Rapid heating combined with extended high-temperature exposure will cause phase separation, elemental segregation, and less-controlled particle morphology.
Standard rapid-heating and rapid-cooling synthesis commonly produces high decomposition temperatures, increased precursor mobility, and mixed phases.
Extremely high temperatures or overly long high-temperature exposure can override kinetic trapping regardless of heating-ramp adjustment.
The relationship between heating or cooling rate and phase purity depends on elemental composition and precursor chemistry.
Low-temperature formation of single-phase HEA nanoparticles can be governed by stochastic principles and inhibition of precursor mobility.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies slow cooling as a source of excessive mobility, but the intervention treats slower heating as mobility-suppressing without explaining why increasing time during one part of the thermal cycle has the opposite kinetic effect.

The baseline attributes increased mobility and mixed phases to rapid heating and cooling, whereas the intervention proposes slower heating as the mobility-limiting condition. This heating-rate direction is neither reconciled nor supported by the cited evidence.

The adverse comparison condition is described both as rapid heating and cooling and as rapid heating with extended high-temperature exposure; rapid cooling and extended high-temperature dwell are materially different protocols.
